title: Annotatio II §.III (2): Justin & Gregory Nyssen — earthly substance with external holiness
pass_a_gloss: (2) An earthly substance affected with a certain holiness is at least implicitly introduced by a Writer a little older than Irenaeus, St. Justin Martyr, when near the end of the Second Apology to Emperor Antoninus he recounts his time’s Christian custom of celebrating the Supper thus: After the President has given thanks and the people have acclaimed, those who among us are called Deacons or Ministers give to each of those present what they may take of bread and wine; and this food is called by us Eucharist; for we do not take them as common bread, nor as a common cup. To the same sense Gregory of Nyssa in the Oration on the Baptism of Christ: Bread, he says, is at first common, but consecrated or sanctified through the mystery is called the body of Christ. That both speak of bare external holiness — the former by the name common bread, i.e. to be contradistinguished as destined and set apart by word and prayers for holy use; the latter by similitudes soon added from the holiness of oil for holy use, of water in baptism, even of the temple and stones from which a temple is to be built — he explains plainly enough.
pass_b_english: (2) Justin (near Irenaeus’s senior) describes deacons giving bread and wine called Eucharist — not taken as common bread or cup.

Gregory of Nyssa: bread starts common, then consecrated is called Christ’s body — both mean bare external holiness (set apart by word and prayer; like oil, baptismal water, temple stones), not a second metaphysical substance.
source_text: (2) Substantiam terrenam sanctitate quadam affectam, Irenæo paulò vetustior Scriptor, S. Justinus Martyr, saltem implicitè inducit, quando Apol. secunda ad Anton. Imperat. prope finem, Christianorum sui temporis consuetudinem celebrandæ Cænæ hisce recenset: Postquam Præses gratias egit & acclamavit populus, illi, qui à nobis dicuntur Diaconi, seu Ministri, dant cuique præsentium quod sumant de pane & vino; & hoc alimentum à nobis vocatur Eucharistia; non enim ut vulgarem panem, neque ut vulgare poculum ea sumimus. Eundem in sensum Greg. Nyssenus in Orat. de Baptis. Christi: Panis, ait, initio communis est, sed per mysterium consecratus, vel sanctificatus, dicitur corpus Christi. Utrumque verò de nuda externa sanctitate verba facere, prior, appellatione vulgaris panis, i. e. destinato separatoque, per verbum & preces ad sanctum usum, contradistinguendi; posterior verò adjectis mox Similitudinibus nonnullis, à Sanctitate olei ad sanctum usum, aquæ in baptismate, quin templi lapidumque, ex quibus templum exstruendum est, petitis, disertè satis explicat.
